q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT bar, COUNT(*) AS total_frequents FROM frequents GROUP BY bar), CTE2 AS (SELECT bar, AVG(price) AS average_price FROM serves GROUP BY bar), CTE3 AS (SELECT bar, MAX(times_a_week) AS max_times_a_week FROM frequents GROUP BY bar), CTE4 AS (SELECT * FROM frequents ORDER BY drinker), CTE5 AS (SELECT CTE3.bar, CTE4.drinker FROM CTE3, CTE4 WHERE CTE3.bar = CTE4.bar AND CTE3.max_times_a_week = CTE4.times_a_week), CTE6 AS (SELECT bar, MIN(drinker) AS min FROM CTE5 GROUP BY bar) SELECT CTE.bar, CTE.total_frequents, CTE2.average_price, CTE6.min FROM CTE, CTE2, CTE6 WHERE CTE.bar = CTE2.bar AND CTE2.bar = CTE6.bar ORDER BY CTE.total_frequents

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent due to the different methods they use to determine the 'most regular drinker' at each bar. Q1 uses a subquery to find the drinker with the highest times_a_week, while Q2 uses a CTE to find the drinker with the highest times_a_week and then another CTE to find the minimum drinker name among those with the highest times_a_week. This can lead to different results if there are multiple drinkers with the same highest times_a_week.
counterexample_dsp: A test database with two bars, each having two drinkers with the same highest times_a_week, but different drinker names.
